events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: David's Oath of the Horatii
events.blurb: A 36-year-old French painter, working in Rome, exhibited at the Paris Salon a sharply geometric, classically themed canvas of three Roman brothers swearing on their father's outstretched swords to fight for their city. Women wept in the shadows on the right. The painting's stark rejection of Rococo decoration and its austere civic virtue appealed exactly to the mood of a country five years from revolution.
events.revealBlurb: 1784 — Jacques-Louis David, exhibited at the Salon of 1785. Painted in Rome; shipped to Paris. David would become the leading painter of the French Revolution, personally designing the Tennis Court Oath as a commemorative picture and painting Marat dead in his bath.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Fall of Monte Cassino
events.blurb: After four separate offensives spanning five months, Polish troops raised their flag over the ruins of a hilltop monastery that had been reduced to rubble by an Allied bombing raid — finally cracking a mountain defensive line that had blocked the Allied advance up a peninsula for half a year and cost over 43,000 casualties across all the assaulting armies.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1944. Polish Corps commander General Anders had promised his men they would fight for Poland in the west since the Soviet Union had taken the east. Over 900 Polish soldiers died in the final assault. The monastery's Benedictine monks had evacuated its art treasures months earlier; the abbey itself was empty during the famous Allied bombing of February 15.

events.title: Japan's Formal Surrender
events.blurb: Aboard a battleship anchored in a bay surrounded by an Allied fleet of 250 ships, representatives of a defeated empire signed the instrument of its unconditional surrender on a folding table set up on the deck, ending the largest armed conflict in human history after six years of fighting across every ocean and every inhabited continent.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 1945 — USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. General MacArthur opened the ceremony: "We are gathered here to conclude a solemn agreement." The signing took 23 minutes. Japan's foreign minister, in top hat and tails, signed on behalf of the government. Allied Commander MacArthur used five pens to sign, giving them to survivors of Bataan, Corregidor, and others.

events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Arab Spring Begins
events.blurb: A 26-year-old Tunisian fruit vendor, after a municipal inspector confiscated his cart for the second time and, by his family's account, publicly slapped him, set himself on fire outside the provincial governor's office. He died in hospital 18 days later. Protests over his treatment — coordinated partly through Facebook and Twitter — became a revolution that spread to Egypt, Libya, Syria, Yemen, and Bahrain within weeks.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 2010 — Mohamed Bouazizi in Sidi Bouzid. Tunisia's president fled to Saudi Arabia on January 14, 2011. Hosni Mubarak resigned in Egypt on February 11. The movement's ultimate trajectory varied dramatically: consolidated democracy in Tunisia for a decade, civil war in Syria and Libya, authoritarian restoration in Egypt.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Bannister's 4-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old medical student in his final year of training, racing on a windy Oxford track in a university-versus-amateur competition, ran a mile in 3 minutes and 59.4 seconds — the first human ever to break the four-minute barrier. The record stood for 46 days. His pacers, who trailed off at the halfway and three-quarter marks on a pre-arranged plan, were athletes the newspapers had not noticed. Sport doctors had warned a sub-four mile might be physiologically impossible.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1954 — Roger Bannister at Iffley Road track. Pacers: Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy of Australia broke Bannister's record 46 days later. Bannister beat him in the "Mile of the Century" race at the Vancouver Commonwealth Games in August 1954 — both running sub-four.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Oprah's "You Get a Car!"
events.blurb: An American daytime talk-show host opened her show's 19th-season premiere by giving a brand-new compact sedan to each of 276 audience members who, she said, had been nominated by loved ones as desperately needing a new vehicle. She turned to a different audience section and shouted: "You get a car! You get a car!" each audience member in turn. The sustained joy — and the full-volume shouting — became a lasting cultural moment captured in countless memes and parodies.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2004 — Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show. The cars were Pontiac G6 sedans donated by General Motors, which covered the ~$7 million cost as a promotion. Audience members were reportedly shocked to discover the IRS expected them to pay tax on the "gift" of around $7,000.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Avengers: Endgame Opens
events.blurb: The 22nd film in a 11-year sprawling superhero cinematic universe opened in theatres worldwide, bringing together nearly every hero introduced across the previous decade for a time-travel battle against a cosmic villain. The three-hour film made $1.2 billion in its opening weekend alone — by a comfortable margin, the largest opening in box-office history — and eventually surpassed Avatar's decade-old record for highest-grossing film of all time. It marked the end of an "Infinity Saga" and the conclusion of multiple central characters' arcs.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 2019 — Avengers: Endgame from Marvel Studios. Final box office: $2.798 billion. The film required some 2,500 visual effects shots; about 90 percent of what appears on screen is CGI. Robert Downey Jr.'s Iron Man had kicked off the Marvel Cinematic Universe 11 years earlier.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Drake Completes Circumnavigation
events.blurb: An English privateer, captaining one of five ships that had set out three years earlier on a raiding expedition against Spanish New World colonies, returned to his home port with holds full of Spanish silver and the honour of being the first Englishman — and second captain ever — to circumnavigate the globe. His queen personally knighted him on the deck of his ship. Spain's ambassador demanded his execution; the queen politely declined.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1580 — Sir Francis Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Plymouth. Only his ship of the original five returned, with 59 of the original 164 men. The queen's share of the plunder more than doubled her annual government revenue for that year.

events.title: King James Bible Published
events.blurb: An English translation committee of 47 scholars, working in six sub-committees across three cathedrals, completed a new authorized English Bible commissioned seven years earlier by the English king at a church conference. Rather than abandon earlier translations, they drew liberally on William Tyndale's sixteenth-century Protestant version. The resulting text shaped English-language literary style so pervasively that its phrases are still in routine use four centuries later.
events.revealBlurb: 1611 — commissioned at the Hampton Court Conference, 1604. James I of England (and VI of Scotland) authorized it. Its prose cadences, largely inherited from Tyndale, influenced Shakespeare, Milton, Blake, Dickens, and Lincoln. Its Old Testament translation was done primarily at Westminster and Cambridge; the New at Oxford.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Anand Released
events.blurb: A terminally ill man facing lymphosarcoma of the intestine spends his remaining months arguing that life is worth celebrating — while his doctor-friend records him in a notebook — in a film whose two leads delivered career-defining performances on opposite emotional registers. Its final line, spoken after death, became among the most quoted in Hindi cinema.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1971 — directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, dialogues by Gulzar. Rajesh Khanna was at the absolute peak of his popularity; Amitabh Bachchan was still a supporting player. The film reportedly made Amitabh Bachchan weep on set during the final sequence — which Mukherjee kept in the film.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel. He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: Atari 2600 Launches
events.blurb: For the first time, a home console used interchangeable cartridges — meaning the same hardware could play a new game every week. Atari sold 250,000 units in the first months at $199 apiece. Within three years the living room had replaced the arcade as the primary venue for video games.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 1977 — Atari released the Video Computer System (renamed 2600 in 1982). By 1982, 15 million 2600s had been sold and the console was generating $2 billion in annual revenue.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: University of Bologna Founded
events.blurb: A self-organized guild of foreign students in a northern Italian city hired local scholars to lecture them on civil and canon law, and the informal arrangement crystallized into something new: a chartered community with legal privileges, standardized exams, and a governing rector elected by the students themselves. It is considered the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world.
events.revealBlurb: 1088 — date traditionally given, though the institution evolved over decades. The students were mostly the sons of wealthy families across Europe; they often hired the professors directly and fined them for being late to class. Petrarch, Dante, Copernicus, and Erasmus all studied there.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Alien and Sedition Acts Signed
events.blurb: President John Adams signed four statutes that extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years, empowered the president to expel foreigners deemed dangerous, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious" criticism of the government. The laws were aimed largely at French immigrants and Republican newspaper editors who opposed the Federalist administration.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1798 — Philadelphia (the Sedition Act, last of the four). Twenty-five people were arrested and ten convicted under the Sedition Act — all of them Jefferson's supporters. Jefferson himself quietly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions arguing states could nullify federal law.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: September 11 Terrorist Attacks
events.blurb: That morning, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers commandeered four commercial aircraft and flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and a fourth — whose passengers revolted and forced the plane down — into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the United States' longest wars, a sweeping reorganization of domestic security, and a generation of political consequence.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania. The North Tower stood 102 minutes after impact; the South Tower collapsed first, 56 minutes after being hit, because the plane struck lower floors. The 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence of state sponsorship by any foreign government.

events.title: Lehman Brothers Collapses: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.blurb: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history, with over $600 billion in assets — triggering a global financial panic that erased more than $10 trillion in U.S. household wealth and produced the worst economic downturn since the 1930s. The failure stemmed from the firm's enormous exposure to mortgage-backed securities tied to a collapsing housing market.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 2008 — New York City. The Federal Reserve and Treasury had just rescued Bear Stearns and Fannie Mae but declined to backstop Lehman. The Dow dropped 504 points that day — and lost another 33% over the next three months. TARP, a $700 billion bank rescue program, was signed into law 19 days later.

events.title: COVID-19 National Emergency Declared
events.blurb: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency, unlocking $50 billion in federal disaster funds to respond to the coronavirus pandemic, which had by then spread to 49 states and killed dozens of Americans. The pandemic would ultimately claim over 1.1 million American lives — more than any war in the country's history — and shut down schools, businesses, and public life for over a year.
events.revealBlurb: March 13, 2020 — The White House. The first confirmed U.S. case had been detected just 53 days earlier. Within weeks, American unemployment reached 14.7% — the highest since the Great Depression — as roughly 22 million jobs vanished in two months.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.blurb: A force of 10,000 Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a Persian expedition of 25,000 troops and cavalry on a coastal plain 40 kilometres northeast of Athens. The Athenian commander had tricked the Persians into overextending on the wings, then enveloped them. The Greek victory preserved Athenian independence against the greatest military empire of the age and, by extension, the classical Greek cultural project. A runner dispatched to Athens with news of the victory is said to have expired on arrival.
events.revealBlurb: c. September 12, 490 BCE. Commander: Miltiades. The runner Pheidippides is the foundation myth of the marathon road race; the distance — 42.195 km — matches the run from the battlefield to Athens only coincidentally, set for the 1908 London Olympics.

events.title: Battle of Gaugamela
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's force of 47,000 defeated a Persian imperial army of perhaps 250,000 in the open plains of a Mesopotamian valley. The Macedonian king personally led the decisive cavalry charge at a gap that opened in the Persian centre when its king's bodyguards shifted to counter a feint on the wings. The Persian king fled the field, abandoning his empire; he was murdered by his own satraps a year later. Alexander entered Babylon as the new lord of Asia.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 331 BCE — Alexander III of Macedon vs. Darius III of Persia. Alexander had refused his general Parmenion's advice to attack at night; he reportedly said "I will not steal my victory." Darius fled to Bactria, where he was killed by his cousin Bessus — who was then captured and executed by Alexander.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Chandragupta Founds the Maurya Empire
events.blurb: A north Indian commander, probably trained and advised by the pragmatic political philosopher Kautilya, overthrew the kings of the northern Indian Magadha region and established a new dynasty that would go on to unify most of the subcontinent under a single government. Within a generation his grandson would convert to Buddhism after a bloody campaign of conquest and spread it across Asia. The empire's founding is conventionally placed in the 320s BCE.
events.revealBlurb: c. 321 BCE — Chandragupta Maurya. Kautilya's treatise "Arthashastra," an early work of statecraft written in Sanskrit, is sometimes called an Indian counterpart to Machiavelli. Chandragupta is said to have later abdicated, embraced Jainism, and died through religious starvation in southern India.

events.title: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.blurb: A Visigothic king and his army, frustrated by failed negotiations with a Western Roman emperor for lands and subsidies, entered Rome itself through an unguarded gate and spent three days pillaging. It was the first time the city had been sacked since the Gauls in 390 BCE — eight centuries earlier. The city's wealth and status had made it symbolically untouchable; the shock rippled through the Mediterranean world. Pagans blamed Rome's adoption of Christianity; Augustine wrote "The City of God" partly in response.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 410 CE — Alaric I the Visigoth. The emperor Honorius was safely in Ravenna, the western capital since 402. The historian Jerome wrote from Bethlehem: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Alaric died of illness a few months after the sack.

events.title: Janet Jackson Super Bowl Halftime
events.blurb: An American pop singer, performing with Justin Timberlake at a Super Bowl halftime show, experienced a "wardrobe malfunction" — Timberlake pulled at her leather bustier at the end of their duet, exposing her right breast for 9/16ths of a second on live television. The incident produced an estimated $550,000 in regulatory fines, congressional hearings, and a lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court. It effectively launched YouTube (co-founder Jawed Karim said later that the desire to re-watch the moment inspired the site). Timberlake's career was barely touched; Jackson's was permanently diminished.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2004 — Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show in Houston. The word "wardrobe malfunction" entered the English language. A 2020 retrospective documentary drew new attention to how asymmetrically the American public had blamed Jackson.

events.title: Kanye Interrupts Taylor Swift
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Chicago rapper walked onstage at a New York awards show as a 19-year-old country-pop singer was beginning her acceptance speech for Best Female Video, took the microphone from her, and declared that another nominee deserved to win. The interruption shocked the audience; the singer stood silently holding the award. It seeded a long-running and increasingly baroque public rivalry between the two performers that would include her several songs about him, his 2016 song about her, and a leaked phone call.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2009 — Kanye West interrupting Taylor Swift at the MTV VMAs. The other nominee Kanye was championing: Beyoncé. Beyoncé won the night's top award and gave her acceptance time back to Swift. The moment has replayed in the Swift-West feud for over 15 years.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
events.blurb: An English writer who had been educating herself in French enlightenment philosophy published a 300-page treatise arguing that women appeared inferior only because they received inferior education, and that a rational republic required the rational education of both sexes. It was attacked, praised, and influential on both sides of the Atlantic. She died five years later from complications after childbirth.
events.revealBlurb: January 1792 — Mary Wollstonecraft. The child she died giving birth to was Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein. Her husband, William Godwin, published an honest memoir after her death that destroyed her reputation for a century.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes
events.blurb: A 29-year-old women's tennis champion beat a 55-year-old former men's Wimbledon champion in straight sets at a televised exhibition match at a Houston indoor arena, before 30,000 spectators and an estimated 90 million television viewers worldwide. The older player had spent months mocking women's tennis in the press; he entered the arena on a rickshaw pulled by models in skimpy outfits and gave her a Sugar Daddy lollipop at the net.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1973 — Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 at the Houston Astrodome. King had threatened to boycott the US Open unless prize money was equal; Forest Hills agreed in time for the tournament that August — the first Slam to do so.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Malala Yousafzai Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Pakistani girl, who had been shot in the head by a Taliban gunman on her school bus two years earlier for publicly advocating for girls' education, became the youngest-ever winner of the world's most prestigious peace prize. She shared the award with an Indian child-rights activist. She had been giving anonymous interviews to the BBC since age 11; she was now a household name.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 2014 — Malala Yousafzai and Kailash Satyarthi. She was attacked on October 9, 2012 in Swat Valley and underwent multiple surgeries in the UK. Her autobiography had been published the previous year. She was 11 years below the previous youngest laureate.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Fair Housing Act Signed
events.blurb: One week after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., Congress passed and the president signed legislation outlawing discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing. The bill had been stalled for two years; King's death and the rioting that followed pushed it through. It closed the third major gap in civil rights law, after employment (1964) and voting (1965).
events.revealBlurb: April 11, 1968 — Lyndon Johnson. Informally called the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Enforcement remained toothless for decades; the Department of Housing and Urban Development did not gain meaningful investigation powers until the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: Rapper's Delight Released
events.blurb: Three rappers from the New York metro area, assembled by an independent label, released a 15-minute track over a bassline lifted from a recent disco hit. It was the first hip-hop single to reach the U.S. Billboard Top 40. The culture it came from had been thriving in parks and clubs around the Bronx for six years; this record introduced it to mainstream white America and set rap on the path from subcultural movement to dominant global genre.
events.revealBlurb: September 1979 — Sugarhill Gang on Sugar Hill Records. The bassline was from Chic's "Good Times"; Chic's Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards sued and received co-writing credit. The track went platinum in the US and hit #3 in the UK.

events.title: Freddie Mercury Dies
events.blurb: A 45-year-old rock singer issued a statement from his London home the previous day confirming the rumors he had been fighting for years: he had AIDS. He died the next evening of bronchial pneumonia resulting from the disease. His band's 1975 operatic epic had just re-entered the UK charts on the back of its use in a film released the previous May, and climbed to number one the week after he died.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1991 — Freddie Mercury of Queen. The film was "Wayne's World"; the song "Bohemian Rhapsody." A tribute concert at Wembley Stadium the following April was broadcast to over a billion people.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Half-Life Released by Valve
events.blurb: Every first-person shooter before Half-Life presented missions as separate levels with loading screens and no coherent world. Half-Life placed the player inside a continuous unbroken environment, told its story entirely through actions the player participated in, and won more than 50 Game of the Year awards. Critics later divided gaming history into "pre-Half-Life" and "post-Half-Life" eras.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1998 — Valve's debut game released for Windows. Budgeted for lifetime sales of 180,000 copies, it sold 212,000 in the United States alone by year-end and ultimately over 9 million copies. It spawned Counter-Strike as a fan mod. Valve used the revenue to build Steam.

events.title: Grand Theft Auto V Released
events.blurb: A crime game set in a fictionalised Los Angeles earned $800 million on its first day and $1 billion within three days — the fastest any entertainment product in history had reached that figure at that time. Guinness certified six world records on launch day. More than a decade later it continues to generate revenue through its online component.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 2013 — GTA V launched for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It broke six Guinness World Records including fastest entertainment property to gross $1 billion. The game has sold over 200 million copies. GTA Online continues to generate over $1 billion annually.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Fallingwater Completed
events.blurb: A 70-year-old American architect completed a weekend house for a Pittsburgh department-store owner, cantilevered dramatically over a waterfall in rural western Pennsylvania. The design — with horizontal reinforced-concrete terraces seemingly floating over the rock and water — reimagined what residential architecture could be and became a singular icon of 20th-century organic architecture. The cantilevered decks began sagging within years; an expensive 21st-century restoration saved the house.
events.revealBlurb: 1937 — Frank Lloyd Wright for the Kaufmann family in Bear Run, PA. The Kaufmanns had expected the house to sit across from the waterfall looking at it; Wright insisted on placing it over the water. Wright won the Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1941 and the AIA Gold Medal in 1949.

events.title: Virgil's Aeneid
events.blurb: A 51-year-old Roman poet died with his commissioned national epic not quite finished, asking on his deathbed that the unfinished manuscript be burned. The emperor he had spent a decade writing it for overruled him. The twelve-book poem traced the mythical origins of Rome to a Trojan prince fleeing the burning city. It became, and remains, the canonical literary masterpiece of Latin civilization.
events.revealBlurb: 19 BCE — Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Emperor Augustus saved the text. Virgil's funeral procession was attended by the emperor himself. Dante took Virgil as his guide through Hell and Purgatory in The Divine Comedy; Milton modeled Paradise Lost on the Aeneid.

events.title: Dante Completes Divine Comedy
events.blurb: A 56-year-old exiled Florentine poet completed the third and final part of a long allegorical poem describing his journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, guided by a Roman poet and his earthly beloved. Written in Italian rather than Latin, it pulled the vernacular into literary respectability. He died within months of finishing.
events.revealBlurb: 1320 — Dante Alighieri. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 over factional politics; he never returned. The last 13 cantos of Paradiso were missing for months after his death until his son Jacopo found them in a secret cavity in a wall, supposedly after Dante appeared in a dream.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Globe Theatre Opens
events.blurb: A London acting company, evicted from their original playhouse when their landlord refused to renew the lease, dismantled the building overnight, carried the timbers across the frozen Thames, and rebuilt them into a new circular theatre on the south bank. Their principal playwright and shareholder produced several of his greatest plays on its stage over the next 14 years, until a cannon effect during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.
events.revealBlurb: 1599 — the Lord Chamberlain's Men; William Shakespeare was a shareholder. It burned on June 29, 1613; was rebuilt; was demolished in 1644 under Puritan hostility to theatre. A faithful replica opened in 1997 near the original site.

events.title: Boston Massacre
events.blurb: A confrontation between a hostile crowd of several hundred colonists and a squad of nine British soldiers on a snow-covered Boston street ended with the soldiers firing into the mob, killing five men. The deaths — including Crispus Attucks, a formerly enslaved sailor of African and Indigenous descent — were immediately weaponized as propaganda, with Paul Revere producing an engraving that circulated throughout the colonies.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1770 — King Street, Boston. John Adams, who would become America's second president, defended the British soldiers in court and won acquittals for six of the eight — calling it one of the best things he ever did for his country. Attucks is often called the first American to die for independence.

events.title: Franco-American Alliance
events.blurb: A French-American treaty signed in Paris transformed the American rebellion into a global war. France, which had been secretly funneling weapons and volunteers to the rebels through front companies, formally recognized American independence, committed its navy to the war, and in return secured commercial terms with the new republic. Spain joined the next year, the Netherlands the year after, and Britain soon found herself fighting Europe's great powers on multiple oceans.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1778 — Treaty of Alliance, Paris. Benjamin Franklin, the Americans' chief diplomat, had worked the French court for two years in a coonskin cap that French aristocrats found exotically charming. France's participation in the war contributed significantly to its own fiscal collapse a decade later.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer.
