The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: The Breakfast Club Released
events.blurb: A film about five high-school students from different cliques stuck together for a Saturday detention in the school library opened in American theatres. The cast — a nerd, a jock, a princess, a rebel, a weirdo — talked, argued, and bonded over 97 minutes in a script tight enough that one actor later claimed much of it felt improvised. The film defined a style of introspective teen comedy-drama the decade would become known for. It grossed $45 million on a $1 million budget.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1985 — John Hughes directing Emilio Estevez, Molly Ringwald, Judd Nelson, Ally Sheedy, and Anthony Michael Hall. Hughes had written the script in a single weekend, 1982. The final fist-pump shot, set to Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)," became iconic.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Friends Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour NBC sitcom about six young adults — a food chef, an aspiring actor, a paleontologist, a masseuse, a restaurant hostess, and a data processor — sharing two Greenwich Village apartments premiered to middling reviews and moderate ratings. The show would run ten years, cement the demographic of "twentysomething in Manhattan" as a comedy staple, and command an unprecedented $1 million per episode per cast member in its final season. Its title sequence featured six friends splashing in a fountain.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 1994 — Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc, Matthew Perry, David Schwimmer. Created by Marta Kauffman and David Crane. The cast negotiated as a union, a strategy that pushed their salary to the stratosphere. Perry died in 2023 at 54.

events.title: Archimedes' Principle of Buoyancy
events.blurb: A Greek mathematician established that an object submerged in fluid is buoyed upward by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — a principle explaining why objects float or sink and allowing the density of irregular objects to be measured precisely. The insight reportedly struck the mathematician while stepping into a bath, causing him to run through the streets in excitement.
events.revealBlurb: c. 250 BCE — the "Eureka" bath story was first told by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, so historians treat it sceptically. What is not disputed is that Archimedes wrote it all down carefully in On Floating Bodies, one of the oldest surviving works of physics. He also calculated an approximation of pi accurate to three decimal places.

events.title: Electromagnetic Field Equations Published
events.blurb: A Scottish physicist unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single mathematical framework of four equations, showing that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa — generating self-propagating waves that travel at the speed of light. The equations predicted that light was an electromagnetic wave and implied the existence of radio waves, infrared radiation, and other forms not yet observed.
events.revealBlurb: 1865 — James Clerk Maxwell's paper was read to the Royal Society in December 1864. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed the existence of radio waves in 1887, nine years after Maxwell died of cancer at 48. Richard Feynman called Maxwell's equations "the most significant event of the 19th century" — a bold statement given the century's competition.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Penicillin Discovered
events.blurb: Returning from vacation, a bacteriologist noticed a petri dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mold that had dissolved the surrounding bacterial colonies into clear halos. He cultured the mold — Penicillium notatum — and determined it produced a substance lethal to bacteria, naming it penicillin.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Monterey Pop Festival
events.blurb: A three-day rock festival on a California coastal fairground — the first major rock festival of the decade and the template for what came later — introduced American audiences to a left-handed guitarist recently returned from London, a young Otis Redding, and Janis Joplin. The left-hander, during his set, laid his guitar on the stage, knelt over it, and set it on fire with lighter fluid. The audience had not imagined such a thing was possible.
events.revealBlurb: June 16-18, 1967 — the guitarist was Jimi Hendrix, on the closing Sunday. Monterey Pop Festival drew 200,000 people. The Mamas & the Papas had organized it; proceeds went to charity. Paul McCartney recommended Hendrix and The Who to the organizers.

events.title: Thriller Released
events.blurb: A 24-year-old singer released his sixth studio album, a collection of nine tracks deliberately designed so every one could be a single. The 14-minute title track's horror-film music video, featuring choreographed zombie dancing, premiered the following December on a cable channel that had until recently been reluctant to play Black artists. The album became, and remains, the best-selling album of all time.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1982 — Michael Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones. It has sold over 70 million copies worldwide. The moonwalk, which Jackson debuted performing "Billie Jean" at Motown's 25th-anniversary TV special 3.5 months after release, was not actually his invention.

events.title: Nirvana's Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from the Pacific Northwest released their second album — recorded for $65,000, with a cover showing a naked infant underwater reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. The album's lead single had been written, according to the band, to sound "like the Pixies" and made a mockery of that idea. By January it had displaced Michael Jackson's "Dangerous" at number one and changed what major-label rock sounded like for the rest of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 24, 1991 — Nirvana, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl. The lead single was "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The infant on the cover, Spencer Elden, later sued the band (unsuccessfully) for using his image.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: Little Rock Nine
events.blurb: Nine Black teenagers, escorted by federal troops, walked through the front doors of an Arkansas capital's previously all-white high school, three weeks after the governor had called out the National Guard to bar them. The images of the 101st Airborne at the schoolhouse door — bayonets fixed — broadcast on the nightly news forced a hostile public to confront massive resistance.
events.revealBlurb: September 25, 1957 — Central High School, Little Rock. President Eisenhower federalized the entire Arkansas National Guard to override Governor Orval Faubus. One of the nine, Elizabeth Eckford, was famously photographed walking alone through a screaming mob on an earlier attempt.

events.title: James Meredith at Ole Miss
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Air Force veteran, after a year of legal battles, became the first Black student to enroll at a Mississippi university with a deep segregationist tradition. His arrival on campus sparked a night-long riot by a mob of 3,000 whites that killed two people and injured hundreds. Federal marshals and troops protected him through graduation.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1962 — Oxford, Mississippi. President Kennedy sent 30,000 federal troops, the largest domestic military deployment since the Civil War. Governor Ross Barnett had personally tried to block Meredith four times. Meredith graduated with a degree in political science.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: Minecraft Officially Released
events.blurb: A game with no story, no tutorial, no win state, and graphics that looked like 1989 asked players to punch trees and build whatever they wanted. It became the best-selling video game of all time. Schools adopted it as an educational tool. A generation learned their first lessons about architecture, resource management, and server administration inside it.
events.revealBlurb: November 18, 2011 — Minecraft version 1.0.0 launched at Minecon in Las Vegas. Microsoft acquired developer Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion. By 2025 the game had sold over 350 million copies — more than twice the second-best-selling game.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale Mode Launches
events.blurb: Epic released a free-to-play mode in which 100 players parachuted onto an island and fought until one survived, funded entirely by cosmetic purchases. Within two months it had more players than any game in history. It didn't invent the battle royale genre, but it perfected the business model — and convinced the rest of the industry that free-to-play with optional cosmetics was the future.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2017 — Fortnite Battle Royale launched free on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One. Within two months it had 45 million players. The game's in-game concerts — including Travis Scott's 2020 event with 12.3 million simultaneous viewers — redefined live entertainment.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Patented
events.blurb: A textile worker patented a multi-spindle spinning frame that allowed a single operator to spin eight threads simultaneously — a number later increased to 120. The machine slashed the cost of cotton yarn and displaced the hand-spinning cottage industry within a generation.

events.title: Stockton-Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A 40-kilometre railway built to carry coal from the inland pits of County Durham to the shipping harbour at Stockton-on-Tees opened with a locomotive designed by a former colliery engineer pulling a 30-wagon train of coal, flour, and 600 passengers. It was the first public railway to use a steam locomotive for passenger service. Horse-drawn wagons continued to share the line for its first decades.
events.revealBlurb: September 27, 1825 — engineer George Stephenson, his locomotive "Locomotion No. 1." On the opening day Stephenson himself drove the engine, reaching a giddy top speed of 24 km/h. The railway ran until nationalization in 1948.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First CT Scanner
events.blurb: A British engineer at a small electronics company introduced the first clinical computed tomography scanner, which used X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images of the inside of a patient — the first medical imaging breakthrough since the X-ray 76 years earlier. Early scans took hours and resolved only the head; within a decade the technology could produce full-body scans in minutes.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1971 — Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; first clinical scan at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, Wimbledon, London. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel with Allan Cormack. EMI funded the research from its Beatles albums revenue.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Babe Ruth's Called Shot
events.blurb: A Yankee slugger, facing a Cubs pitcher in game 3 of a World Series at a Chicago ballpark amid heckling from the dugout and the crowd, gestured with his bat toward the center field bleachers and then, on the next pitch, hit a home run that landed roughly where he had pointed. Whether he had actually "called" the shot is debated among eyewitnesses and film analysts to this day; teammates and opponents offered contradictory accounts for decades. The legend has long since outgrown the facts.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1932 — Babe Ruth at Wrigley Field. Opposing pitcher: Charlie Root, who denied the called shot to his death. An 8mm home movie shot by a Chicago fan, discovered in 1992, shows Ruth pointing — but whether to the outfield or the Cubs dugout is still contested.

events.title: Michael Jordan's First Retirement
events.blurb: Three months after winning his third straight NBA championship and four months after his father had been murdered in a highway robbery, the 30-year-old best basketball player in the world held a press conference announcing his retirement from the game. He had "lost the desire to play," he said. Months later he was playing minor-league baseball for a Chicago White Sox affiliate. He would return to the NBA 17 months after his retirement, winning three more championships.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1993 — Michael Jordan. His AA baseball season with the Birmingham Barons ended with a .202 batting average. His return to the NBA, announced March 18, 1995 with the two-word press release "I'm back," drew him to four more championships (1996, 1997, 1998) before a second retirement, then a third comeback with the Washington Wizards.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Munich Agreement
events.blurb: Four heads of government met through the night in a grand hall in southern Europe and handed over a democratic nation's border region to an aggressive neighbour — without inviting a single representative of that nation to the table. The leader who returned home waving the signed paper declared it meant peace; within six months the entire country had been swallowed.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1938 — Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, and Mussolini signed over the Sudetenland at 1:30 AM. Chamberlain's "peace for our time" paper became history's most mocked diplomatic document. Czechoslovakia's envoys waited in an anteroom and were simply informed of the result.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: D-Day Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. A massive deception operation convinced enemy commanders the real target was 300 kilometres further east.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 1944 — Operation Overlord. Eisenhower carried a note in his pocket taking full blame if it failed. The "Mulberry" artificial harbours, towed across the Channel in pieces, unloaded two million tons of supplies in the months that followed. The first soldier ashore on Sword Beach was a British piper playing "Blue Bonnets Over the Border."

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Nuremberg Verdicts
events.blurb: An international tribunal delivered verdicts against 22 senior leaders of a defeated regime after ten months of proceedings that introduced "crimes against humanity" as a concept in international law — finding twelve guilty of offences for which they would be executed, and establishing the principle that following government orders is not a defence against such charges.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1946. Hermann Göring cheated the hangman by swallowing a cyanide capsule hours before his scheduled execution — a capsule no one ever satisfactorily explained. The other ten were hanged on October 16. Three defendants were acquitted. The tribunal's procedural framework became the model for every subsequent international war crimes court.
